card.hook: Up on a bluff called the Mire, 119 m above the sea, the whole bay spreads out below you with the neighbouring islands dotted beyond. The height is the reason to come, and the thick walls make great frames.
card.stand_here: The phone icon sits in the middle of the fort grounds, so once you're inside you're already there. For the big view, walk to the northern bastion and face out over the bay and the islands.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the bay and the sweep of the walls. Use 1x for the bastion and the cactus garden, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the far islands.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line and keep it level, then tap the far islands and slide a touch darker so the sky stays blue.
card.best_time: Midday sun can wash out the view, so morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the colour of the sea.
card.selfie_here: Take it in the exotic garden inside the fort grounds. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the fort's walls over your shoulder, with the blue horizon in front of you.
card.ask_someone: For a shot with the fort behind you, ask a passer-by to stand on the old Tête Rouge battery (on the path toward the restaurant near the beaches), facing the fort on the opposite hill, while you stand between them and the fort. The whole fort may not fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Check which parts of the grounds are open when you arrive, as access may be ticketed or limited. Hold your phone away from the wall edge when you lean out.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the bay, then get close and find a cactus with the sea sitting behind it.
card.good_to_know: A first fort, Fort Louis, was built here between 1777 and 1779, and British forces destroyed it in 1809. The present fortress rose on its ruins, starting in 1816, with the bastioned design finished in 1867. It never saw battle and was used as a penitentiary instead. Today it holds a museum about the Saintes and a botanical garden of local succulents, with iguanas.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon sits in the middle of the fort grounds, so once you're inside you're already there. For the big view, walk to the northern bastion and face out over the bay and the islands.

card.hook: You've just stepped off the ferry, your legs are still doing the boat wobble, and there's a church a short walk away waiting to be your first photo of Terre-de-Haut.
card.stand_here: Try Place du Gouverneur Lion, the ferry-landing square, and face the church front. It's the likely spot but not a sure one, so check on the ground that you can see the whole front before you start shooting.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole church front in one frame. If people or parked scooters stop you stepping back, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the bell tower and the entrance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the church on one of the vertical lines so the tower stands up straight, not leaning.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front. Midday sun can look flat and bright, so check the result on your screen.
card.selfie_here: Try the church's grand front steps, with the weathered stone façade rising behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and switch to 0.5x so the façade fits over your shoulder. This one is a suggestion, so see how the steps look on the day.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the end of the shop-lined street that leads down to the ferry port, facing the church, while you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the street, but this is a working place of worship, so ask locally before you go inside. Watch for scooters passing while you step back for the wide shot.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the tower perfectly upright and not a single scooter in it, then one close-up of the tower. Bonus points if the scooters cooperate.
card.good_to_know: The parish was dedicated to the Virgin of the Assumption to mark the French victory over English troops on 15 August 1666. The church has been a listed national heritage monument since 31 December 1979. The 2004 earthquake destroyed the bell tower, and it was later rebuilt, with the fourth of its four bells installed on 23 April 2006.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Try Place du Gouverneur Lion, the ferry-landing square, and face the church front. It's the likely spot but not a sure one, so check on the ground that you can see the whole front before you start shooting.

card.hook: Picture a tropical bay with not a single boat in it. That's Pompierre Beach, where boats aren't allowed in, so your photo stays clean and uncluttered.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the sand at Pompierre Beach, and face out toward the bay and the offshore rocks. Walk a little way along the sand until a palm trunk or a carbet (the small shelters) sits on one side of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sweep of sand, palms and bay into one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the cove, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pierced rocks.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line, then tap the bright sand and slide it a touch darker so it doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the sand. The beach is described as fairly uncrowded in general, so you've got a good chance of an empty frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sand where the tall coconut palms meet the sea, with the bay open behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it so the palms and turquoise water fit over your shoulder. If the sun is strong, the picnic tables and benches in the palm shade at the back of the beach make a cooler spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the access path above the beach, where the whole bay opens out, to take your photo while you stand on the sand below with the palms beside you.
card.rules_and_safety: Coconuts can fall, so take care when standing or sitting under the palms. Check locally for any closures or restrictions before you go. Seaweed (sargassum) has affected the beach in some reviews, so the view may change.
card.challenge: Can you frame a palm trunk on one side, a line of pale sand leading the eye, and the pierced rocks sitting in the gap?
card.good_to_know: The beach runs for about 800 metres along Pompierre Bay, and the bay is a classified natural site under a French law of 2 May 1930. The little islet of Les Roches percées sits offshore and shelters the bay from the trade winds. If you fancy a higher view, the Batterie Caroline trail is on foot only, so bring sturdy shoes and water.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the sand at Pompierre Beach, and face out toward the bay and the offshore rocks. Walk a little way along the sand until a palm trunk or a carbet (the small shelters) sits on one side of your frame.

card.hook: Picture a round green hump sitting in the bay, as if it parked itself there just to pose for your photo. That's Îlet à Cabrit, and it's happy to be the star.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 350 m south-west of the island. Face north-east and the whole islet is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the island plus lots of sky and sea. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Go 2x-5x (depending on your phone) only if you want to pick out the hilltop or one little cove.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a line and keep it level, because tilted sea looks odd.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and nicer colour on the hill and the water. Midday sun can flatten the view and make the sea glare.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the stone wall beside the Fort Napoléon parking area, near the top of Morne Mire (the road up from town). One sunset guide calls it a favourite view of Îlet à Cabrit. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and turn so the bay and islet are over your shoulder. Check it looks right once you're there.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the island itself and its fort remains may be restricted or ticketed, so check local information before you go.
card.challenge: Add a boat or a bit of shoreline in the foreground, so the island gets a sense of size and your photo looks like a postcard.
card.good_to_know: The island is about 1.2 km from east to west and 750 m from north to south. Its highest point is Morne Joséphine, at around 90 m. France built a fort on the hilltop in 1777, later called Fort Joséphine. The British kept it after they occupied Les Saintes in 1809. It was later a penitentiary from 1851 and a quarantine station from 1871.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 350 m south-west of the island. Face north-east and the whole islet is right in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: A sunset guide calls this its favourite view of Îlet à Cabrit, and the Fort Napoléon ramparts are described as looking out over the bay toward the islet.

card.hook: Boats are always coming or going at Mouillage, and behind them a hillside of bright creole houses stacks up like a box of crayons. It's the oldest village on Terre-de-Haut, and it's hard to take a dull picture here.
card.stand_here: Stand near Rue Jean Calot, about 190 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and you'll look across to the harbour and the village.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole harbour and hillside in. Then switch to 1x for a more natural view. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pick out a single boat or a painted house front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water along the bottom third and keep the horizon level, then tap the houses so they look nice and bright.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. The port is busiest when cruise ships or ferries are in, so expect a crowd then.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with a big view, try the ramparts of Fort Napoléon, which look out over the whole bay of Terre-de-Haut, with Mouillage on the shore below. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little out to the side so the bay sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The ship-bow house is still someone's home, so photograph it from the street and keep a respectful distance.
card.challenge: Find a boat that lines up against the painted houses, then take one shot with the boat and one without. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Mouillage is the oldest village on Terre-de-Haut and home to the main port of the Îles des Saintes. Look out for the 'Bateau des îles', a house shaped like a ship's bow that Adolphe Catan built in 1942. The old gendarmerie is now the archipelago's tourism office, handy if you want local advice.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Rue Jean Calot, about 190 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east and you'll look across to the harbour and the village.

card.hook: Most spots hand you a monument to aim at. Anse Mire just gives you a curve of coast, a bit of sea and a whole lot of sky, and that's plenty.
card.stand_here: Head to Ruelle de l'Anse Mire, about 200 m north-west of the bay, right where the phone icon sits. Face south-east and you've got the whole shoreline in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the bay. Go to 0.5x if you want more coastline and sky in one shot, then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has it) to crop in on the bit of shoreline you like best.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line instead of the middle, so the curve of the bay runs diagonally across the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon is best, when the light is softer on the water. Midday sun makes the sea glare and flattens everything.
card.selfie_here: Walk down to the sand at Anse Mire beach and use the front camera at 0.5x with the wooden boat-shaped house over your shoulder. The turquoise water and wooden houses make a great backdrop, and the beach is sheltered from the wind.
card.rules_and_safety: Manchineel (mancenillier) trees grow on the beach, so don't shelter under them in the rain because they're toxic. Access to the shore and paths can vary, so check local conditions before you go.
card.challenge: Snap the bay wide with a few people in it as tiny figures, then see whose frame gives the best sense of scale.
card.good_to_know: Anse Mire is a bay on the north side of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes archipelago in the Caribbean. The bay itself is the star here, not a single building. Take a few shots in a row, because small changes in the water and clouds can change the whole picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Ruelle de l'Anse Mire, about 200 m north-west of the bay, right where the phone icon sits. Face south-east and you've got the whole shoreline in front of you.

card.hook: Most spots on the map come with a crowd. Anse Crawen comes with sea, shoreline, a big open sky and hardly anyone else in your picture.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map at Anse Crawen, about 200 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. Want a tighter frame? Just stroll a little closer.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and switch on the gridlines. Then try 0.5x to fit in loads of sky and sea. To pick out a boat, a rock or a stretch of shore, use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) instead of walking.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then drag the slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour, and wipe your camera with a soft cloth first because sea air leaves a film.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the water. Midday sun can look harsh, so make the picture a little darker if you're there then.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with a view, climb to the summit of Le Chameau (309 m) and stand by the stone tower. A hiking guide describes a 360° view from up there that includes Anse Crawen below, so use the front camera, try 0.5x and see if you can get the beach behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Near Anse Crawen, avoid manchineel trees (marked with red paint) because their sap causes burns, especially when it rains. It's also the least inhabited part of the island, so be considerate of anyone living nearby.
card.challenge: Keep the horizon dead level on a gridline, then add a rock or the edge of the shore in the front so your photo has depth.
card.good_to_know: Anse Crawen is a quarter on the south-western side of Terre-de-Haut, in the Îles des Saintes. It's the least inhabited part of the island, so it feels calmer than the busier stops on the map. No Underground, tram or bus stops are listed here, so start from the more populated parts of the island and head south-west.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map at Anse Crawen, about 200 m south-west of the subject, and face north-east. Want a tighter frame? Just stroll a little closer.

card.hook: Picture a wall of dark, ridged stone dropping straight into bright blue water. That's Pain de Sucre, the best-known rock on Terre-de-Haut, and it looks great on a phone screen.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 330 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. The rock and the bay will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to show the rock sitting in its bay. Then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the vertical basalt columns. Use 0.5x only if you walk down to a beach and want sand or water filling the bottom of the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the rock, then slide the brightness a touch darker so the sky and white sand don't wash out and the dark stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and better texture on the columns. Midday sun flattens the rock and makes the sea glare. If you're after beach colours, mid-to-late morning is recommended.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plage du Pain de Sucre, the postcard beach that shows up most often in photos of Terre-de-Haut. Stand on the sand, switch to the front camera, and keep the sugarloaf hill over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to fit more in, and check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: For a different angle, stand on the coastal path toward Pointe Bois-Joli with the Pain de Sucre hill behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot you from a few steps back along the path.
card.rules_and_safety: Check access conditions for individual beaches or paths on the day.
card.challenge: Take the rock at 1x, then again at 2x or more, and see if you can spot the moment the columns start to look like organ pipes.
card.good_to_know: Pain de Sucre sits in a mostly residential quartier in the south-western part of Terre-de-Haut, in Les Saintes, Guadeloupe. The quartier is a natural anchorage, and the rock plunges into the bay. Two small white-sand beaches, Petite Anse du Pain de Sucre and Anse Devant, are part of the area and make a pale foreground.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 330 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. The rock and the bay will be right in front of you.
